children: By Theo Francis and Corrie Driebusch
Here's what we know about Anthropic's various shareholders-and the rights they have-in front of one of the most anticipated intial public offerings of the year.

Class A shares: Voting shares held by early investors and employees of the company, and the shares for sale in the IPO. Rather than require all early Class A shareholders to wait the traditional 180 days before selling shares, Anthropic revealed its plans to allow some shares to be sold earlier. Class A shares get dividends and have a claim on what's left if Anthropic ever winds down.

Class N shares: Non-voting shares initially held by Anthropic's strategic partners, they generally convert to Class A if sold or transferred. Anthropic plans to use additional N shares to further its public-benefit mission. They get dividends and have an economic claim on Anthropic.

Class T: Anthropic's Long-Term Benefit Trust has a single Class T share that carries no regular vote, gets no dividends and has minimal economic interest, but has the right to fill a majority of seats on Anthropic's board.

Class F: The company's founders will have the power to appoint the remaining directors and determine most other shareholder votes through control of a single Class F share that automatically has 50.1% of voting power for matters submitted to stockholders generally. No dividends, minimal economic interest.

Class E: These will later go to employees other than co-founders, with only limited voting rights. Not transferable but can be redeemed by the company in some circumstances; no dividends and minimal economic interest.
